title: Table 16.05 Summary of the main features of Lynch syndrome
tablehtml:
Feature

Syndrome characteristics

Syndrome MIM number(s)

120435

Associated malignant tumours

Lynch syndrome–associated malignancies include cancers of the colorectum, endometrium, stomach, small bowel, ovary, gallbladder, hepatobiliary tract, pancreas, kidney, brain, prostate, skin (sebaceous carcinoma), urothelial-lined urinary tract including renal pelvis, ureter, and bladder, and probably sarcomas (to be confirmed)

Associated benign tumours

Colorectal adenomas, gastric and duodenal / small bowel adenomas and other polyps, urothelial papillomas of the urinary tract, cutaneous lesions (sebaceous adenomas and sebaceomas, but not sebaceous hyperplasia) and keratoacanthomas

Cancer-related inheritance

Autosomal dominant (with reduced penetrance)

Chromosome location

Germline pathogenic variants affecting a DNA mismatch repair gene:

MSH2 (2p21)

MLH1 (3p22.2)

MSH6 (2p16.3, only 300 kb from MSH2)

PMS2 (7p22.1)

Some individuals have substitution variants / deletions / inversions involving adjacent genes, such as EPCAM (2p21), which affects the neighbouring MSH2 gene, or LRRFIP2 (3p22.2), which affects neighbouring MLH1

Protein product–associated pathway

DNA mismatch repair

diagnosis: Distinct subclonal loss pattern in MMR protein immunohistochemistry
legend: MSH6 immunohistochemistry of a colorectal adenocarcinoma showing distinct subclonal loss of MSH6 in the tumour (with sharply demarcated regions showing the presence or absence of staining in the tumour cells while having normal staining in the stromal cells in both regions). Depending on the case, this could represent a secondary phenomenon (e.g. secondary subclonal loss due to somatic mutation in the MSH6 coding mononucleotide tract in a tumour that is MLH1 and/or PMS2 deficient) or a primary phenomenon (due to either germline [constitutional] MSH6 mutation or somatic MSH6 alteration inactivating both MSH6 alleles).

diagnosis: Indistinct heterogeneous staining pattern in MMR protein immunohistochemistry
legend: Indistinct heterogeneous staining can happen with all MMR proteins, but most commonly with MLH1 and MSH6. When it happens with MLH1 staining, and the PMS2 staining is normal, it should be interpreted as intact; if the PMS2 staining is lost, then the indistinct heterogeneous staining pattern with MLH1 could be a reflection that the dMMR (loss of PMS2) is likely due to MLH1 gene abnormality, and MLH1 staining should be regarded as abnormal. Similar situation can happen with MSH6 indistinct heterogeneous staining: if the MSH2 staining is lost, then the case is dMMR (most likely due to MSH2 gene abnormality), and the indistinct heterogeneous MSH6 staining should be regarded as abnormal as well. If the MSH2 staining is normal (i.e., isolated MSH6 indistinct heterogeneous staining), then close clinical correlation is suggested; if there is a clinical desire to know the Lynch syndrome status, germline (constitutional) testing should be pursued; if immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy is a consideration, then MSI testing should be pursued.

Weak and patchy MSH6 immunoexpression in rectal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy is likely a secondary phenomenon, and not reflective of MSH6 gene alteration. If there is any clinical concern, the test should be repeated on the pretreatment biopsy sample.

diagnosis: A suggested algorithm for colorectal cancer testing for Lynch syndrome
legend: MMR, mismatch repair; MSI-H, high level of microsatellite instability; MSI-I, indeterminate level of microsatellite instability; MSS, microsatellite-stable.
